title: Mallow and the Miniature Mountain
markdown:
Aethelgard’s towers poked the sky like grey fingers, and valleys hung like green necklaces from the windy tops. In that breezy land lived Mallow, an ogre as big as a barn, moss-coloured, fireplace eyes, who preferred old books about clouds and the patterns on butterfly wings. Stomping was not for him.

His best friend was Marble, a plump speckled hen whose cluck could shake teacups and who was, frankly, a little bossy. They had a gigantic problem that rumbled in their tummies: zero coins. Not a copper. Not even enough for honey-cakes and roasted veg.

“Oh, pickles!” Marble fluffed. “My beak is vibrating. I need a proper supper. Not dewdrops on dandelions. My tummy is singing honey-cakes.”

Mallow’s mossy brow creased like a well-loved map. “Mine is doing a solo called Empty. Distressing melody.” He peeked at a land bursting with sparkle and coins. A sigh, soft as a whisper.

A proclamation, a scroll so large it made its own weather, came down from the tallest tower. Village contest: the most marvellous miniature mountain. First prize: fifty gleaming gold coins.

Fifty coins. A mountain of cakes. Worms enough for Marble to swim in. The extra-fluffy bedspread Mallow had been dreaming about. His eyes lit like twin hearths. He loved mountains. He lived near them. A tiny one? Better than a rumbling tummy.

They trotted to the square, huge feet surprisingly quiet on cobbles. Elf Nessa was already there, moonlight hair, jaw set, sketching a teeny peak with a charcoal twig. Mallow nodded; she was too busy with angles to nod back.

Then the show: Eldrin the Wizard, beard like spun moonlight, twilight robes, a competitive sparkle. “My dear Morwen,” he announced to the air, for Morwen the Witch—thundercloud hair, a smile that could curdle milk—was setting her easel, cauldron bubbling suspicious violet, “I shall naturally win. My mountains possess celestial grandeur, touched by cosmic whispers.”

Morwen cackled, pebbles in a tin. “Cosmic whispers? Bah. Mine have the raw untamed power of the earth. They will tower, pulsing with the planet’s heart.” The politest, most competitive wizard-versus-witch rivalry Aethelgard had seen. Spells crackling. Robes swishing.

Mallow watched, a slow smile. He could not out-magic them. Their work fizzed and hummed. He could out-think them. While Eldrin conjured perfume-clouds and Morwen sculpted humming rocky lumps, Mallow sat at the edge of the square. He needed a companion for his mountain: one that understood quiet growth.

A tiny shimmering beetle scuttled across a fallen pinecone, shell like a miniature emerald, a determined zig-zag, as if it knew where it was going. “That one,” Mallow whispered to Marble, pointing a massive mossy finger. He scooped it into a small acorn kept for emergencies, usually tasty nuts. “My muse. It understands the silent language of stone and soil.” The beetle would be guardian, a living heart for sculpted peaks.

Meanwhile Eldrin and Morwen practised artistic interference. Eldrin’s mist drifted, quite by accident, over Morwen’s prize boulder, making it slippery. Morwen sent a gust that tumbled Eldrin’s snowcap into an undignified pile. “A minor atmospheric anomaly,” sniffed Eldrin, adjusting his moonbeam beard. Morwen narrowed her eyes. “That dragon is trying to be subtle. It is not its strongest subject.”

Mallow simply built. Fallen pine needles for trees, arranged like a gardener’s dense forest. Smooth grey stones balanced into natural ledges. Dandelion fluff for a wispy peak, a cloud snagged on a summit. At the centre, the acorn and beetle, a tiny living sentinel.

When his turn came, Eldrin and Morwen exchanged smug glances. They expected the gentle ogre to present something boring. The judges approached, monocles gleaming. Mallow’s mountain was not loud with magic. It was alive. Needles whispered. Stones looked ancient. The beetle, peeking from its acorn, surveyed its domain with quiet dignity.

The judges, usually serious and prone to doom, found themselves smiling. They had seen power. They had not seen such thoughtful craft, nature’s own artistry. Mallow, whom everyone thought slow, had made a miniature world of peace.

The fifty gold coins were his. Eldrin and Morwen stood speechless, bickering forgotten. “At least his beetle seemed well-behaved,” huffed Eldrin, beard a little less sparkly. “No unpredictable surges.” Morwen nodded, grudging respect. “Understated. Natural harmony.”

Mallow shared a generous portion with Marble, who clucked approval. Supper was, indeed, a mountain of honey-cakes, and the plumpest worms Marble had ever seen. Nessa, passing with her unused sketches, paused long enough to look at the beetle’s peak and, for the first time that afternoon, smiled at something that was not her own charcoal. The bedspread could wait until morning. The tummies had stopped their solos.
audience: children aged 9-10, amusing distant-lands fantasy for independent readers
